name: Nikhil Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What happens on an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and new enough on the blast-hole drill that I still measure twice before I set the mast. I operate it at a large mine, check the ground with the shift lead and record each hole before the blasting crew takes over. Secondary school was the end of my formal education, but I use an AI phone assistant every day to explain unfamiliar machine terms, then check the manual or a person. My partner Tom repairs bicycles, our two children are grown, and my higher mine pay has given us more than six months of savings. I like the neat row of holes after a shift; I dislike waiting for someone to correct a mistake I could have asked about sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the drill crew that a bit of AI in the office won't change the ground under our rigs. I already use a phone assistant to look up unfamiliar terms, and I can see why that saves time when the answer is checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still a junior operator, so I don't confuse a clever explanation with being good at drilling. The strong pay could disappear if I keep making slow set-ups, even with no big AI change. Tom's bicycle work and our savings give us room, but I want to earn my own place here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the drill and practise mast set-up with the shift lead every Friday. I'd save the next bonus instead of buying the used boat Tom and I looked at last month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel comfortable with the small tools already in my pocket. The harder feeling is wanting to prove I belong at the mine before anyone judges me by my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What went wrong on a recent set-up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lined the mast with a mark that had shifted after rain. The shift lead caught it before I started the hole, and we reset it together. I wrote the correction on the page I carry in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put off the boat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom and I saw one beside the river that looked affordable until we added storage and repairs. We laughed and drove home without it. The bonus is better in our savings while I'm still proving myself.

say: I'd say **small AI tools** can save time if someone checks the answer.
I'd tell the crew the **drill ground** still has to be read by people on site.
think: I'm **junior** and still slow setting the mast, whatever happens to office work.
Tom's bicycle income and our **savings** help, but I want to keep earning the mine wage.
do: Practise **mast set-up** with the shift lead each Friday while staying on the drill.
Save the next **bonus** instead of buying a used boat.
feel: **Comfortable** with small tools, but eager to prove I belong on the rig.
S0.quote: I'm still a junior operator, so I don't confuse a clever explanation with being good at drilling.
fieldNote: He separates daily **AI explanations** from the physical judgment needed to set a drill mast safely.
His **strong savings** give him room, yet he places personal weight on becoming competent at a trade he joined late.

steps.text: Continue drill shifts and practise mast set-up with the shift lead
Save the next mine bonus instead of buying a used boat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software will take more of the plans, purchase orders and drilling records first. I'd want the mine to show operators how its new plan is checked against actual rock before the screen starts sending us to the next hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI daily, so I'd be curious to test a digital hole log. A junior drill operator can be tempted to trust an elegant plan more than wet ground. That is the part I would watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the first supervised digital-log trial if the mine offers one. In the first year of the change, I'd record any mismatch between its hole position and the survey marker and take it to the shift lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested, even a little pleased to have a useful new skill. I feel uneasy only when someone treats a neat screen as proof the ground is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the mismatch show up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the stake beside the planned hole, where the surveyor's mark and the screen position should agree. I've seen a stake kicked loose by a tyre. I'd photograph the marker and ask before putting steel into the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daily phone use help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me learn the words and ask better questions. It doesn't make me a surveyor. I'd still have the shift lead or surveyor settle a disputed position.

say: I'd say **plans and records** change before a robot takes a drill into wet ground.
I'd ask for a **field check** of any digital plan before operators follow it.
think: I'd enjoy testing a **digital hole log** because I already use AI daily.
I worry a **junior operator** could trust a tidy plan over a warning on the ground.
do: Volunteer for a **supervised digital-log trial** if the mine offers one.
Record **marker mismatches** and take them to the shift lead in the first year.
feel: **Interested** in the skill, with unease when a screen outranks physical evidence.
S1.quote: A junior drill operator can be tempted to trust an elegant plan more than wet ground.
fieldNote: Nikhil welcomes **digital records** but wants a human check against survey markers and changing ground.
His willingness to volunteer reflects **daily AI use**, while his worry centres on false confidence in a junior operator.

steps.text: Join a supervised digital hole-log trial if the mine offers one
Record hole-marker mismatches for the shift lead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AGI in 2028 could do the mine's planning and records cheaply, while robot drills come roughly in 2031. I'd ask which operator posts will remain during the change and what training is actually paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60, I could use thinking AI to learn more quickly, but the drill seat could still go around my 63rd year. I have savings and my partner Tom's bicycle business, yet neither is a promise that we can stop paid work. I would rather test another job while this wage exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training office this month about a paid drill-maintenance place and enrol if one is offered. If robot drills remove our posts in 2031, I'd apply for maintenance assistant vacancies at the two local mines that run similar rigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel scared of losing a high wage just after I got it. Having three years between the thinking change and the robots makes me restless to learn, rather than unable to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of maintenance appeals to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like tracing why a drill vibrates differently before a fault becomes serious. I don't know enough to repair one, which is why I want a paid place beside the fitters. The hands-on work could face robots too, but I could use it while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tom do with the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd work out how long they cover our bills without my wage, including the shop's quiet months. Tom would keep the bicycle bench open if customers came. We wouldn't spend the whole pot on a course that the mine could have paid for.

say: I'd say **2028 AGI** reaches planning first, with robot drills expected around 2031.
I'd ask for **paid training details** and a count of operator posts that may remain.
think: At **63**, a robot drill could remove a wage I still need.
Our **savings** buy time, but they do not guarantee retirement or steady bicycle income.
do: Ask the **training office** about paid drill-maintenance places and enrol if offered.
Apply for **maintenance assistant posts** at local mines if robot drills remove operator jobs.
feel: **Scared** for the wage, yet restless to learn before robot drills arrive.
S2.quote: I have savings and my partner Tom's bicycle business, yet neither is a promise that we can stop paid work.
fieldNote: He sees a **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robot drilling as a short training window.
His **daily AI habit** supports learning, but he does not mistake it for maintenance qualifications or a secure retirement.

steps.text: Enrol in paid drill-maintenance training if the mine offers a place
Apply for local maintenance assistant posts if robot drills remove operator jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people that AGI in 2031 gives a longer period to watch the planning jobs change before robot drills arrive around 2034. I'd ask the mine to publish which equipment roles it expects to keep, with dates for any training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 when thinking AI arrives and 66 for the robots. That feels close to retirement until I picture our actual expenses and how uneven Tom's shop can be. Five years lets me build a second skill, if the place is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take one paid maintenance module each year if the mine makes those available, starting with hydraulics next spring. I'd stay on the drill while learning and compare technician vacancies at nearby mines before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful rather than rushed. Five years helps me train, but it does not turn an uncertain mine job into a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why start with hydraulics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can already see the hoses and pressure readings each morning, but I don't know how to diagnose the system. A fitter showed me a leak last week and explained what would happen if we ignored it. That is a real lesson I can build on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply for a technician job immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I met the requirements. I'd look at adverts now and ask the training office what certificate they require. I don't want to leave a good drill wage just to become an unqualified helper somewhere else.

say: I'd say **2031 AGI** changes planning before robot drills threaten operators around 2034.
I'd ask for **dated role figures** and specific training places.
think: At **66**, I might still need paid work when robots reach the drill.
Five years could build a **second skill**, if the course is genuine and paid.
do: Take a paid **hydraulics module** next spring if the mine offers one.
Keep **drill shifts** while comparing local technician vacancies.
feel: **Watchful**, with more room to learn but no certainty about future income.
S3.quote: Five years helps me train, but it does not turn an uncertain mine job into a pension.
fieldNote: Nikhil proposes **one module yearly**, connecting the longer warning to a workable pace alongside paid shifts.
He checks **local vacancies** because a course has value only if it opens work at his mine or nearby.

steps.text: Take a paid hydraulics module next spring if offered
Continue drill shifts while comparing local technician vacancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade before AGI in 2036 gives us a chance to see which technology earns its place at the mine. Robot drills around 2039 would come when many of today's operators are older, but younger workers need a longer answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 for the thinking change and 71 when robots could drill like us. I might have retired before robot drills arrive in 2039, though I cannot name the year without checking my partner Tom's bicycle shop income and our bills. I would still be curious to learn tools that help me work safely now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd review our household budget with Tom every autumn and keep a note of my likely retirement income. I'd try a verified drill-monitoring tool on the job if the mine offers training, while continuing paid shifts as long as I can do them safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel patient about my own work in this version. I feel less easy for the younger operators, whose wages have many more years to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the monitoring tool trustworthy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a trained fitter and an operator to compare its warnings with the drill's actual vibration for a few months. If it catches something useful, I'd use it. I don't need a shiny screen for its own sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mention the younger operators?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One of them helped me learn the rig and has just taken on a mortgage. I may be out by 2039, but he could still need twenty years of work. I'd want the mine to give him a path before the drill seat disappears.

say: I'd say **2036 AGI** leaves time to test what actually helps the mine, with robot drills around 2039.
I'd ask for **younger workers** to have a longer training path than an exit date.
think: I would be **68** for AGI and around 71 for robot drills.
I might retire first, but **shop income** and household costs make that uncertain.
do: Review the **household budget** and likely retirement income with Tom each autumn.
Try a **verified drill-monitoring tool** with training if the mine offers it.
Continue **paid drill shifts** while I can do the work safely.
feel: **Patient** about my own options, with concern for younger operators' longer working lives.
S4.quote: I might have retired before robot drills arrive in 2039, though I cannot name the year without checking my partner Tom's bicycle shop income and our bills.
fieldNote: He keeps his **retirement timing** open until household figures and health offer firmer evidence.
Even in the slow case, his **curiosity about tools** survives, while concern for younger operators becomes stronger.

steps.text: Review household budget and retirement income with Tom each autumn
Learn the drill-monitoring tool if the mine offers training
Continue paid drill shifts as long as the work remains safe

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robot drills could arrive when I'm 63 and I may still need this good wage. A paid maintenance place with a real opening at the end would help me act now. I have savings and my partner Tom's bicycle business, yet neither is a promise that we can stop paid work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I would enjoy learning another machine or system. I would, provided someone checks my work while I learn. Being 58 doesn't make the curiosity disappear; it makes me less willing to waste time on a course with no job.

headlineQuote: Being 58 doesn't make the curiosity disappear; it makes me less willing to waste time on a course with no job.
portrait: At **58**, Nikhil is a junior blast-hole drill operator still learning to set the mast safely.
He and partner Tom have **strong savings**, grown children and income from a bicycle repair business.
He uses **AI daily** to explain machine terms, then checks answers with a manual or colleague.
He seeks **paid maintenance training** under faster change while keeping retirement timing open in the slow case.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because robot drills around 2031 could remove his wage at about age 63.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid maintenance place** leading to a real vacancy would let him learn while his drill wage continues.
